records.literal_gloss: And these [are the] sons of the province who came up from [the] captivity of the exile, whom had carried into exile Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon to Babylon, and they returned to Jerusalem and Judah, each to his city,

en.L: And these [are] the sons of the province who came up from the captivity of the exile, whom Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon had carried into exile to Babylon, and they returned to Jerusalem and Judah, each to his city,
en.B: These are the people of the province who came up out of the captivity of the exiles whom Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon had carried away to Babylon. They returned to Jerusalem and Judah, each to {{gender:their|his}} own town,
en.R: This is a list of the people of the province of Judah who came back from exile. Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon had taken them away as prisoners to Babylon. Now they returned to Jerusalem and the rest of Judah. Each family went back to its own town.

decisions.choice: the sons of the province: the people of Judah, now a province of the Persian empire
decisions.reason: Judah was no longer a kingdom but one of the provinces of the empire, as in Nehemiah 1:3 and 11:3. "Sons of" here means the people belonging to it.

decisions.choice: the list of those who returned
decisions.reason: The same list stands in Nehemiah 7:6-72, where Nehemiah finds it in the records of those who first came back. The two copies differ in a number of names and figures; the notes on the verses below give the main differences.

decisions.choice: each to his city: each family to its home town
decisions.reason: The families went back to the towns their ancestors had lived in, as the town names in verses 21-35 show (compare Nehemiah 11:3).

decisions.choice: Readable adds "of Judah" and "as prisoners"
decisions.reason: Readable names the province and says what being carried into exile meant, and breaks the long sentence.

decisions.choice: Zerubbabel and Jeshua: the governor of David's line and the high priest
decisions.reason: Zerubbabel was a grandson of King Jehoiachin (1 Chronicles 3:17-19) and became governor of Judah (Haggai 1:1). Jeshua son of Jozadak was the high priest (Ezra 3:2); Haggai and Zechariah call him Joshua (Haggai 1:1; Zechariah 3:1). They lead the rebuilding in chapters 3-6.

decisions.choice: Nehemiah and Mordecai: other men of the same names
decisions.reason: These are leaders of the first return. They are not Nehemiah the governor, who came about ninety years later (Nehemiah 2:1), nor Esther's cousin Mordecai, who lived in Susa (Esther 2:5).

decisions.choice: eleven names here, twelve in Nehemiah 7:7
decisions.reason: Nehemiah 7:7 has twelve leaders: it adds Nahamani and has Azariah for Seraiah, Raamiah for Reelaiah, Mispereth for Mispar and Nehum for Rehum. Twelve leaders may stand for the twelve tribes of Israel, as the twelve offerings do in Ezra 6:17 and 8:35.

decisions.choice: the Nethinim: the temple servants, "those given" to the temple
decisions.reason: The word means "the given ones". They were people given to the temple to help the Levites in its work; Ezra 8:20 says David and his officials gave them for the service of the Levites. They may go back to foreigners put to work at the sanctuary, like the Gibeonites who became "cutters of wood and drawers of water for the house of my God" (Joshua 9:23, 27); some names in this list, such as Meunim and Nephusim (verse 50), look foreign. After the return they belonged fully to the community (Nehemiah 10:29).

decisions.choice: the Nethinim (Literal); the temple servants (Balanced, Readable)
decisions.reason: Literal keeps the Hebrew word as a name, as older English Bibles did; Balanced and Readable say what they were.

decisions.choice: Tel-melah, Tel-harsha, Cherub, Addan, Immer: places in Babylonia
decisions.reason: These are settlements where the exiles lived, like Tel-abib by the Chebar canal (Ezekiel 3:15). "Tel" means a mound, the ruin of an old town, on which a new village could be built. Nehemiah 7:61 has Addon for Addan.

decisions.choice: show their fathers' house and their seed: prove their family line
decisions.reason: They could not show from family records which ancestral house they belonged to and that they were descended from Israel. They still came and were counted (verse 60); the question was only their standing.

en.R: Some priests could not prove their families either: the descendants of Hobaiah, Hakkoz and Barzillai. This Barzillai had married a daughter of Barzillai from Gilead and was called by the name of her family.

decisions.choice: Barzillai the Gileadite: the man who helped David
decisions.reason: Barzillai of Gilead, east of the Jordan, brought food to David when he fled from Absalom (2 Samuel 17:27-29; 19:32-40), and David asked Solomon to care for his sons (1 Kings 2:7). A priest married into his family and took its name, so his own priestly line was no longer clear.

decisions.choice: was called by their name: took the name of his wife's family
decisions.reason: "Their" refers to Barzillai's daughters, that is, to his family. Taking the wife's family name may have been for the sake of an inheritance (compare Numbers 36:1-12).

decisions.choice: Readable adds "could not prove their families either"
decisions.reason: The next verse shows that these priests were in the same position as the families of verses 59-60; Readable says so at the start.

source.text: אֵ֗לֶּה בִּקְשׁ֧וּ כְתָבָ֛ם הַמִּתְיַחְשִׂ֖ים וְלֹ֣א נִמְצָ֑אוּ וַֽיְגֹאֲל֖וּ מִן־הַכְּהֻנָּֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: These sought their writing, the ones enrolled by genealogy, and not they were found, and they were defiled from the priesthood.

en.L: These sought their record [among] those enrolled by genealogy, but they were not found, and they were treated as defiled [and excluded] from the priesthood.
en.B: These looked for their entry among those listed in the family records, but they were not found there, so they were barred from the priesthood as unclean.
en.R: They looked for their names in the family records, but the names were not there. So they were not allowed to serve as priests, because they were treated as unclean.

decisions.choice: those enrolled by genealogy: the family registers
decisions.reason: Israel kept written records of families by descent (1 Chronicles 5:17; 9:1; Nehemiah 7:5). A priest had to show that he was descended from Aaron (Numbers 3:10; 17:5).

decisions.choice: defiled from the priesthood: declared unfit and kept out of the priesthood
decisions.reason: The verb means to be made unclean. With "from" it means they were treated as unclean and so excluded from the priests' service. The decision could be changed (verse 63).

source.text: וַיֹּ֤אמֶר הַתִּרְשָׁ֨תָא֙ לָהֶ֔ם אֲשֶׁ֥ר לֹא־יֹאכְל֖וּ מִקֹּ֣דֶשׁ הַקֳּדָשִׁ֑ים עַ֛ד עֲמֹ֥ד כֹּהֵ֖ן לְאוּרִ֥ים וּלְתֻמִּֽים׃

records.literal_gloss: And said the Tirshatha to them that not they should eat from [the] holy of the holy things until [there] stands a priest for Urim and for Thummim.

en.L: And the Tirshatha said to them that they should not eat of the most holy things until a priest stood up for Urim and Thummim.
en.B: The governor told them not to eat any of the most holy food until there was a priest to consult the Urim and Thummim.
en.R: The governor told them they must not eat the most holy food that belonged to the priests. They had to wait until there was a priest who could find out God's answer by using the Urim and Thummim.

decisions.choice: the Tirshatha: a Persian title for the governor
decisions.reason: The word is a Persian title, probably meaning something like "his excellency". It is used of Nehemiah, the governor (Nehemiah 8:9; 10:2). Here it probably refers to Sheshbazzar or Zerubbabel, who led the return (1:8; 2:2; 5:14).

decisions.choice: the most holy things: the parts of the offerings that only priests could eat
decisions.reason: Certain parts of the grain offerings, sin offerings and guilt offerings were "most holy" and could be eaten only by priests (Leviticus 2:3; 6:10, 18, 22; 7:6; Numbers 18:9-10). Excluding these men from them meant not counting them as priests.

decisions.choice: the Urim and Thummim: the lots kept by the high priest
decisions.reason: The Urim and Thummim were kept in the high priest's breastpiece and used to receive the LORD's answer in hard cases (Exodus 28:30; Numbers 27:21; 1 Samuel 28:6). The text implies they were not in use at this time; the question was left until a priest could consult them. What they looked like and how they were used is not known.

decisions.choice: the Tirshatha (Literal), the governor (Balanced, Readable); Urim and Thummim at every level
decisions.reason: Literal keeps the Persian title as a name; Balanced and Readable say what it means. Urim and Thummim have no English equivalent and stay as names; Readable says what they were used for.

source.text: כָּל־הַקָּהָ֖ל כְּאֶחָ֑ד אַרְבַּ֣ע רִבּ֔וֹא אַלְפַּ֖יִם שְׁלֹשׁ־מֵא֥וֹת שִׁשִּֽׁים׃

records.literal_gloss: All the assembly as one [was] four ten-thousands two thousand three hundred sixty,

en.B: The whole assembly together numbered 42,360,
en.R: The whole assembly numbered 42,360 people.

decisions.choice: 42,360: more than the sum of the families listed
decisions.reason: The numbers in verses 3-60 add up to 29,818 (in Nehemiah 7 to 31,089), yet both lists give the same total, 42,360 (Nehemiah 7:66). The total may include people not listed by family, such as women and children, or members of other tribes; or numbers in the lists may have changed in copying, which happens easily with numbers. The text does not say.

decisions.choice: as one: all together, in total
decisions.reason: The phrase means the whole number counted together (Nehemiah 7:66; compare Ezra 3:1).

source.text: מִ֠לְּבַד עַבְדֵיהֶ֤ם וְאַמְהֹֽתֵיהֶם֙ אֵ֔לֶּה שִׁבְעַ֣ת אֲלָפִ֔ים שְׁלֹ֥שׁ מֵא֖וֹת שְׁלֹשִׁ֣ים וְשִׁבְעָ֑ה וְלָהֶ֛ם מְשֹׁרְרִ֥ים וּֽמְשֹׁרְר֖וֹת מָאתָֽיִם׃

records.literal_gloss: besides their male slaves and their female slaves, these [were] seven thousand three hundred thirty and seven; and to them [were] male singers and female singers two hundred.

en.L: besides their male slaves and their female slaves; these [were] 7,337; and they had 200 male singers and female singers.
en.B: not counting their male and female servants, who numbered 7,337; and they had 200 male and female singers.
en.R: Besides these, there were 7,337 male and female servants, and 200 men and women who were singers.

decisions.choice: male and female slaves: servants the families owned
decisions.reason: These were servants who belonged to the households, counted apart from the assembly. That there were one for every six people shows that some families had wealth.

decisions.choice: male and female singers: singers of the households, not the temple singers
decisions.reason: These are not the Levite singers of verse 41, who were men. They were probably singers for feasts and for mourning (2 Samuel 19:36; 2 Chronicles 35:25; Ecclesiastes 2:8). Nehemiah 7:67 has 245.

decisions.choice: slaves (Literal); servants (Balanced, Readable)
decisions.reason: The project's rule for this word: "slave" at Literal, "servant" at Balanced and Readable, with the meaning decision saying that they were owned.

source.text: סוּסֵיהֶ֕ם שְׁבַ֥ע מֵא֖וֹת שְׁלֹשִׁ֣ים וְשִׁשָּׁ֑ה פִּרְדֵיהֶ֕ם מָאתַ֖יִם אַרְבָּעִ֥ים וַחֲמִשָּֽׁה׃

records.literal_gloss: Their horses seven hundred thirty and six, their mules two hundred forty and five,

en.B: They had 736 horses, 245 mules,
en.R: They had 736 horses and 245 mules,

decisions.choice: horses and mules: missing from most Hebrew copies of Nehemiah 7
decisions.reason: In most Hebrew manuscripts Nehemiah 7 has no line for the horses and mules; translations that add it there number it Nehemiah 7:68. Horses and mules were for riding, so few families had them; camels and donkeys (verse 67) carried the loads.

source.text: גְּמַ֨לֵּיהֶ֔ם אַרְבַּ֥ע מֵא֖וֹת שְׁלֹשִׁ֣ים וַחֲמִשָּׁ֑ה חֲמֹרִ֕ים שֵׁ֣שֶׁת אֲלָפִ֔ים שְׁבַ֥ע מֵא֖וֹת וְעֶשְׂרִֽים׃פ

records.literal_gloss: their camels four hundred thirty and five, donkeys six thousand seven hundred and twenty.

en.B: 435 camels and 6,720 donkeys.
en.R: 435 camels and 6,720 donkeys.

decisions.choice: donkeys: the common pack animal
decisions.reason: Donkeys were the ordinary animals for carrying loads and people. The journey from Babylon to Jerusalem took about four months (Ezra 7:9).

source.text: וּמֵרָאשֵׁי֙ הָֽאָב֔וֹת בְּבוֹאָ֕ם לְבֵ֥ית יְהוָ֖ה אֲשֶׁ֣ר בִּירוּשָׁלִָ֑ם הִֽתְנַדְּבוּ֙ לְבֵ֣ית הָֽאֱלֹהִ֔ים לְהַעֲמִיד֖וֹ עַל־מְכוֹנֽוֹ׃

records.literal_gloss: And some of [the] heads of the fathers, in their coming to [the] house of the LORD which [is] in Jerusalem, offered freely for [the] house of God, to set it up on its place.

en.L: And some of the heads of the fathers, when they came to the house of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} which [is] in Jerusalem, offered freely for the house of God, to set it up on its place.
en.B: Some of the heads of families, on coming to the house of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} in Jerusalem, made freewill offerings for the house of God, so that it could be set up again where it had stood.
en.R: When they reached the place in Jerusalem where the temple of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} had stood, some of the family leaders gave gifts freely so that God's temple could be built again in the same place.

decisions.choice: the house of the LORD: the temple site, still in ruins
decisions.reason: The Babylonians had burned the temple in 586 BC (2 Kings 25:9). The returning leaders came to the place where it had stood; the altar was set up first (3:2-3), then the foundation laid (3:10).

decisions.choice: to set it up on its place: to rebuild it on its old site
decisions.reason: The temple was to stand where the first one had stood, as the decree also says (5:15; 6:7).

decisions.choice: Readable says "the place ... where the temple had stood"
decisions.reason: The temple was a ruin when they arrived, so Readable makes clear that they came to its site.

source.text: כְּכֹחָ֗ם נָתְנוּ֮ לְאוֹצַ֣ר הַמְּלָאכָה֒ זָהָ֗ב דַּרְכְּמוֹנִים֙ שֵׁשׁ־רִבֹּ֣אות וָאֶ֔לֶףסוְכֶ֕סֶף מָנִ֖ים חֲמֵ֣שֶׁת אֲלָפִ֑ים וְכָתְנֹ֥ת כֹּהֲנִ֖ים מֵאָֽה׃ס

records.literal_gloss: According to their strength they gave to [the] treasury of the work: gold, darics six ten-thousands and a thousand, and silver, minas five thousand, and tunics of priests a hundred.

en.L: According to their ability they gave to the treasury of the work: gold, 61,000 darics, and silver, 5,000 minas, and 100 priests' tunics.
en.B: As they were able, they gave to the treasury for the work 61,000 darics of gold, {{units:about 3 tons|5,000 minas}} of silver and 100 garments for the priests.
en.R: Each family gave what it could afford for the work: 61,000 darics of gold, {{units:about 3 tons|5,000 minas}} of silver, and 100 sets of clothes for the priests.

decisions.choice: darics: Persian gold coins
decisions.reason: The daric was the gold coin of the Persian empire, first struck under Darius I (522-486 BC), weighing a little over a quarter of an ounce. The writer counts the gift in the coin of his own day. The word could also stand for the Greek drachma.

decisions.choice: minas: a weight of silver
decisions.reason: A mina was fifty or sixty shekels (Ezekiel 45:12), about 1 1/4 pounds, so 5,000 minas weighed about 3 tons.

decisions.choice: Nehemiah 7:69-71 gives the gifts differently
decisions.reason: Nehemiah lists the gifts of the governor, of the heads of families and of the rest of the people: together 41,000 darics, 4,200 minas, 50 bowls and 597 priests' garments. The two accounts cannot be matched exactly.

decisions.choice: darics at every level; minas in a units span (Balanced, Readable)
decisions.reason: The daric is a coin, not a measure, so it keeps its name at every level. Literal keeps "minas"; Balanced and Readable give the modern weight with the mina as the alternative.

source.text: וַיֵּשְׁב֣וּ הַכֹּהֲנִ֣ים וְ֠הַלְוִיִּם וּֽמִן־הָעָ֞ם וְהַמְשֹׁרְרִ֧ים וְהַשּׁוֹעֲרִ֛ים וְהַנְּתִינִ֖ים בְּעָרֵיהֶ֑ם וְכָל־יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל בְּעָרֵיהֶֽם׃ס

records.literal_gloss: And dwelt the priests and the Levites and some of the people and the singers and the gatekeepers and the Nethinim in their cities, and all Israel in their cities.

en.L: And the priests and the Levites and some of the people and the singers and the gatekeepers and the Nethinim lived in their cities, and all Israel in their cities.
en.B: So the priests, the Levites, some of the people, the singers, the gatekeepers and the temple servants lived in their towns, and all Israel lived in their towns.
en.R: So the priests, the Levites, the singers, the gatekeepers, the temple servants and some of the people settled in their own towns. All the other Israelites settled in their towns too.

decisions.choice: some of the people: perhaps those who lived in Jerusalem
decisions.reason: As it stands the verse names "some of the people" without saying where they lived. The Greek book of 1 Esdras, which retells this chapter, says that some lived in Jerusalem and the country around it, which may preserve words lost here; Nehemiah 11:1 says that later only a tenth of the people lived in Jerusalem. The Hebrew is translated as it stands.

decisions.choice: all Israel: the returned community as the people of Israel
decisions.reason: Though most of them were from Judah and Benjamin, the book calls the returned community Israel (3:1; 6:17, where they offer twelve goats "for all Israel").

decisions.choice: Readable says "all the other Israelites" and "too"
decisions.reason: Readable makes clear that the second group is everyone not already named.
